newsitem.title: USA: Lawmakers hope for goodwill from bipartisan trip.
newsitem.headline: Lawmakers hope for goodwill from bipartisan trip.

text.p: Upset with political bickering, name-calling and general nastiness in the House, more than 200 lawmakers travelled to Pennsylvania Friday for a bipartisan retreat aimed at improving human relations.
The group, including House Speaker Newt Gingrich, who has been a lightning rod for partisan attacks, boarded a special train for the first such meeting ever held.

They were accompanied by about 165 spouses and more than 100 children for a weekend of socializing and policy sessions aimed at returning civility to the chamber. The retreat in the chocolate town of Hershey was the largest-ever House gathering off Capitol Hill.
"We're talking about what's gone sour in the House and what we can do to sweeten things up," Colorado Democrat David Skaggs, a main organiser of the retreat, said before lawmakers left town.

Illinois Republican Ray LaHood, another sponsor, said the weekend was just the beginning, not the end, of efforts to improve the poisoned atmosphere in the House. "This is not the solution. It's not the panacea. It's the beginning of people ... building relationships," he said.

No news media will be allowed at the retreat, which is also off limits to lobbyists. The meeting is being funded by a $700,000 grant from the Pew Charitable Trusts, which supports nonprofit education, health and other activities.
The gathering will include talks from historians and more personal sessions aimed at fostering understanding of those with different perspectives.

"Six months ago, I couldn't even spell facilitator and now I am one," said Texas Democrat Charlie Stenholm. He said he did not expect the retreat to bring people together on policy issues but to help them "disagree without being as disagreeable as we are."

Sponsors came up with the idea during the last session of Congress, which was marked by unusually bitter exchanges as Republicans came to power for the first time in 40 years and Democrats tried to adjust to their unexpected minority status.

The session was marred by tie-pulling incidents, a threat of fisticuffs and two partial government shutdowns during a bitter, partisan fight over the budget. Gingrich and House Democratic Leader Dick Gephardt have barely spoken to one another in the past two years.

Decorum had been declining before 1995 as Republicans, led by Gingrich, became more aggressive in challenging the entrenched Democratic leadership. Lawmakers were working longer hours with less time or desire to socialize.

At one time, newly elected House members used to meet at bipartisan orientation sessions at Harvard's Kennedy School of Government but more recently Republicans have held separate meetings sponsored by the conservative Heritage Foundation.
But lawmakers can take some comfort from the fact that while constant bickering on the House floor is uncomfortable, Congress has avoided the physical duels of the last century.
